1. Introduction:-
a.

This judgement arises out of a complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as "NI Act") by the complainant against the accused for dishonour of cheque based on the rental amount accrued as debt.

2. Brief Facts of the Case:-
a.
The case of the complainant in brief is that he is the owner of property bearing No. F-1, Alfa-2, Greater Noida, UP.

The Accused, along with her husband Sh.
Dharmender Singh, approached the complainant for renting the said premises.
A Rent Agreement was executed for the period 01.08.2012 to 30.06.2013 at a monthly rent of Rs. 26,000/-.
The agreement contained a specific clause stipulating that if the accused failed to vacate the premises after 30.06.2013, the rent would be enhanced to Rs. 40,000/- per month.
It is alleged that the accused fell into arrears. b.

To discharge the legal liability of four months of rent (July 2013 to October 2013 calculated @ Rs. 40,000/- pm), the accused issued Cheque No.
852676 dated 31.10.2013 for a sum of Rs. 1,60,000/- drawn on Bank of Baroda, Greater Noida Branch (hereinafter called as "cheque in question").
Upon presentation, the cheque was dishonoured with the remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide returning memo dated 21.01.2014.
A legal demand notice dated 03.02.2014 was sent to the accused, but despite service/deemed service, the accused failed to make the payment within the statutory period of 15 days.
c. Hence, the cognizance in the present matter was taken, and the accused was summoned for the purpose of trial.

In her defence plea, she stated: "Complainant was my landlord and used to visit my house.
He has misused the cheque after stealing the same from my house and forging my signatures."

iii. Dishonour of the Cheque: The cheque must be dishonoured by the bank due to either insufficient funds in the account or because the amount exceeds the arrangement made with the bank.

iv. Notice of Demand: The payee or holder of the cheque must issue a written demand for payment to the drawer, within 30 days of receiving information from the bank regarding the dishonour.

b.
Additionally, the provisions of Sections 139 and 118 of the Act further strengthen the case for the complainant.

Section 139 creates a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque, mandating that the court shall presume, unless proven otherwise, that the cheque was issued for the discharge of a debt or other liability.

Section 118, on the other hand, provides that there is a presumption that every negotiable instrument, including a cheque, was made for consideration, and that it was Ashok Chaddha vs Seema Yadav on 4 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36326660/

The standard of proof for rebutting this presumption is based on the preponderance of probabilities.
d. The court further held that it is not mandatory for the accused to enter the witness box to prove their defence.
They may rely on the evidence presented by the complainant or any other available materials.

The onus to rebut the presumption lies on the accused, but it is important to note that this is an evidentiary burden, not a persuasive one.
e.
Thus, Section 138 operates on the principle of reverse onus of proof - once the complainant proves the essential elements of dishonour, the burden shifts to the accused to raise a plausible defence.
The presumption of guilt is strong, but not irrebuttable, and the accused is entitled to challenge it through a preponderance of evidence.

f. In the backdrop of legal position as enunciated above, it is to be examined by this Court that whether the accused on a scale of preponderance of probabilities has been able to rebut the presumption which has been raised against him and in favour of the complainant, or has been able to demolish the case of the complainant to such extent so as to shift the onus placed upon the accused again on the complainant.

As held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case of Kumar Exports vs Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 SCC 513, the accused can either prove the nonexistence of the consideration and debt by direct evidence or by bringing on record such facts and circumstances,
upon consideration of which, the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt either did not exist or their nonexistence was so probable that a prudent man may act upon the plea that they did not exist.

8. Analysis and Findings:
a. Issue 1 - Issuance of Cheque:
This ingredient pertains to the issuance of the cheque in question itself.
The Accused person had in her notice of accusation denied the signature on the cheques in question.
The cheque in question has been dishonoured owing to insufficiency of funds, and not owing to the signature being mismatched, or different or wrong.
The Court observes a stark contradiction between the stance taken by the accused at the stage of framing of Notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. and the conduct of the defence during the trial.
While the accused initially denied her signature on the cheque in question and claimed forgery, this denial remained a "bald assertion" unsubstantiated by evidence or rigorous cross-examination.
It is settled law that a mere denial in the notice or statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. does not amount to "rebuttal evidence."

The return for insufficiency of funds raises a strong inference that the signature on the cheque matched the specimen signature in the bank's records,
thereby validating the execution of the instrument prima facie.
A perusal of the cross-examination of the Complainant (CW-1) reveals a conspicuous silence regarding the details of the alleged theft and forgery.

The accused did not put any specific questions to the complainant regarding when the cheque was stolen, how the signature was forged, or why the accused did not take immediate legal action upon discovering the theft.

By restricting the cross-examination to a simple suggestion that "the accused has not signed the cheque," without exploring the veracity of the complainant on the allegations of theft and forgery, the defence is deemed to have waived this specific plea.
The accused's claim of forgery is further eroded from the suggestion put forth by her own Counsel during cross-examination.
The Ld. Counsel for the accused suggested to the complainant that the cheque in question was a "Security Cheque."

The plea of a cheque being given as "Security" and the plea of the cheque being "Stolen and Forged"
are mutually destructive.
A security cheque, by definition, implies a voluntary handing over of a signed instrument by the drawer to the payee to secure a liability.
By suggesting that the cheque was given as security, the accused has implicitly admitted to the execution and handing over of the cheque.
The accused cannot be permitted to approbate and reprobate simultaneously; she cannot claim she signed it for security purposes and simultaneously claim her signature was forged.
Section 73 of the Indian Evidence Act empowers the Court to compare the disputed signature with the admitted signature of the accused to satisfy its own conscience.

CW1/3) with the admitted signatures of the accused on the Bail Bonds, the Plea recorded u/s 251 Cr.P.C., and the Statement u/s 313 Cr.P.C. present on the judicial file.
Upon ocular comparison, there is no patent dissimilarity between the disputed signature and the admitted signatures.
The flow, slant, and characteristics of the handwriting appear reasonably similar.
Since the accused failed to lead any defence evidence or examine a handwriting expert to highlight any latent differences, the Court finds no reason to disbelieve the genuineness of the signature.

In light of the cheque being returned for insufficient funds rather than signature mismatch, the self-destructive suggestion of the cheque being a "security" instrument, the failure to cross-examine on the specifics of forgery, and the Court's own comparison finding no patent dissimilarity,
the signature of the accused on the cheque in question is held to be proved.

d. Issue 4 - Legal Notice:
Service of the legal notice is the legal fiction which constitutes the major ingredient of the offence u/s-138 NI Act.

However, the accused has filed her bail bonds with the same address as mentioned on the legal notice, and even the bailable warrants were received back as executed on the same address; hence address on legal notice is correct.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The onus to rebut the presumption lies on the accused, but it is important to note that this is an evidentiary burden, not a persuasive one.
e.
Thus, Section 138 operates on the principle of reverse onus of proof - once the complainant proves the essential elements of dishonour, the burden shifts to the accused to raise a plausible defence.
The presumption of guilt is strong, but not irrebuttable, and the accused is entitled to challenge it through a preponderance of evidence.
The cheque in question has been dishonoured owing to insufficiency of funds, and not owing to the signature being mismatched, or different or wrong.
It is settled law that a mere denial in the notice or statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. does not amount to "rebuttal evidence."
A perusal of the cross-examination of the Complainant (CW-1) reveals a conspicuous silence regarding the details of the alleged theft and forgery.
The accused did not put any specific questions to the complainant regarding when the cheque was stolen, how the signature was forged, or why the accused did not take immediate legal action upon discovering the theft.
The plea of a cheque being given as "Security" and the plea of the cheque being "Stolen and Forged"
are mutually destructive.
A security cheque, by definition, implies a voluntary handing over of a signed instrument by the drawer to the payee to secure a liability.
By suggesting that the cheque was given as security, the accused has implicitly admitted to the execution and handing over of the cheque.
The accused cannot be permitted to approbate and reprobate simultaneously; she cannot claim she signed it for security purposes and simultaneously claim her signature was forged.
Upon ocular comparison, there is no patent dissimilarity between the disputed signature and the admitted signatures.
The flow, slant, and characteristics of the handwriting appear reasonably similar.
Since the accused failed to lead any defence evidence or examine a handwriting expert to highlight any latent differences, the Court finds no reason to disbelieve the genuineness of the signature.
Consequently, the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Ashok Chaddha vs Seema Yadav on 4 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36326660/
8 Instruments Act stands triggered against the accused.

In the present case, after the issue no. 4 is against the accused, the case of the accused is that she does not have any liability towards the complainant and his cheque was misused.
Hence, it is an admitted position that no payment for the cheque in question was made and thus this ingredient of non-payment within 15 days also stands satisfied.
A defence in a Section 138 NI Act case cannot rest on vague accusations.
It requires positive evidence to displace the statutory presumption.
The accused has failed to prove the factum of theft,
failed to produce the alleged police complaint, and failed to explain why no legal action was taken regarding the theft despite her being litigious against the complainant.

the receiving stamp of the police station, or the Daily Diary (DD) entry number.

The accused is not a naive litigant unaware of legal intricacies.
